flags.stem_preview: A respondent dismisses a peer-reviewed study showing modest benefits of a new vaccine schedule by saying: 'The lead author once consulted for the manufacturer...'
flags.answer_preview: Conflict of interest — the respondent treats the lead author's past consulting tie as itself decisive against the vaccine schedule study...
flags.issue: Stance check: a vaccine-schedule example with a conflict-of-interest dismissal frames the COI critique as the fallacy. Per moral_vision §3 + memory feedback_science_voice: vaccines are SCRUTINIZED, institutional capture is named, the COI critique IS often substantively right per the bank. Risk: this question may train students to dismiss legitimate COI concerns about pharma-funded research.
flags.suggested_fix: Use a non-vaccine example for genetic-fallacy / conflict-of-interest illustration. The COI critique CAN be a fallacy if the methodology is sound — but vaccine-schedule research is the exact case where COI concerns are substantive per moral_vision. Pick a different domain (e.g., 'A respondent dismisses a peer-reviewed study on a metal alloy because the lead engineer once consulted for the foundry').

wonder_bias_violations.description: Bank uses 'YouTuber' (31), 'podcast' (38), 'school newspaper' (40), 'debate-club' (31), 'group chat' (3), 'cafeteria/locker/smartphone/TikTok' (~10) as scene-setters. PHILOSOPHY_FRAMEWORK.md §8.3 explicitly lists these on the AVOID list. The flagged set above includes representative samples from each scenery type; the same fix (reframe to knights/scribes/monks/court-debate/cathedral-tower) applies across the remainder. The fallacy block (idx ~340-440) and aesthetics block (idx 40-79) are the densest concentrations.

length_parity_skim_tells_T5_aesthetics.description: T5 aesthetics block has a systematic pattern: the correct answer is ~185 chars while distractors are ~220 chars. A student can skim-pick the shortest choice. Fix is to lengthen correct answers to match distractor density, or trim distractors.

philosopher_name_in_stem.description: About 50 stems mention real philosophers. Per framework: names belong in context. Two acceptable cases: (1) the named figure is a CHARACTER speaking (Tertullian, Descartes, Augustine, Socrates as speaker — broadly acceptable); (2) the named figure's view IS the position being tested and the stem just summarizes 'his view' — this is the problematic attribution case (e.g., 485 Parfit, 526 Parfit, 612 Searle, 613 Locke, 627 Putnam, 657 Putnam, 658 Locke, 643 Searle). The T1 cases (467 Plato, 794 Tertullian, 795 Plantinga, 798 Clifford, 800 Augustine) are problematic because T1 framework specifies 'zero names in stem.'

stance_calibration.description: A few questions have stance-sensitive examples that risk dating, training kids the wrong way, or accidentally undermining the bank's moral vision. 410 (vaccine-COI dismissed as fallacy) is the most load-bearing per memory feedback_science_voice — the COI critique of pharma-funded vaccine research is substantively right per the bank. 368/170 use climate as the canonical 'consensus' example — timestamped per §5 dated-content rule, and contested per memory. 443 frames sovereign-currency-issuer as if MMT-friendly. Replace with timeless or stance-neutral examples.
